body:
The breakdown of political negotiations

By the middle of 1946, the Congress and Muslim League had failed to agree on the implementation of the Cabinet Mission Plan.

The League continued demanding Pakistan and rejected constitutional arrangements that it considered inadequate for Muslim political interests.

Following the breakdown of negotiations, the League decided to organise mass political action in support of its demand.

Direct Action Day: 16 August 1946

The Muslim League announced 16 August 1946 as Direct Action Day.

The purpose was to demonstrate support for the demand for Pakistan through mass political mobilisation.

Large-scale communal riots broke out in Calcutta, now Kolkata, on Direct Action Day. The violence continued for several days and caused thousands of deaths.

The events became known as the Great Calcutta Killing.

The violence intensified distrust between religious communities and made political negotiations more difficult.

Political action and communal violence are not identical

Direct Action Day was a political mobilisation called by the Muslim League. The communal riots that followed involved attacks on people identified by religion. The political call and the violent events must be distinguished, even though they became closely connected historically.

Spread of communal violence

The riots in Calcutta were followed by further communal disturbances in other regions.

Important locations and periods included:

  • Calcutta, August 1946: Major communal riots during and after Direct Action Day.
  • Noakhali, October 1946: Serious communal violence in eastern Bengal.
  • Bihar, late 1946: Communal killings and retaliatory violence.
  • Punjab, early 1947: Escalating communal conflict during the final months of British rule.

Victims belonged to different religious communities in different regions. The spread of violence contributed to fear, displacement and the collapse of confidence in peaceful coexistence.

The deterioration of law and order also increased concern that a rapid political settlement might be necessary to prevent further bloodshed.

Formation of the Interim Government

An Interim Government took office on 2 September 1946, with Jawaharlal Nehru serving as Vice-President of the Viceroy's Executive Council.

The Muslim League did not initially join the government. It entered the Interim Government in October 1946.

However, the participation of both organisations did not eliminate their fundamental constitutional disagreements.

The Constituent Assembly meets

The Constituent Assembly held its first meeting on 9 December 1946.

The Muslim League boycotted its proceedings because it continued to dispute the constitutional arrangement under which the Assembly was functioning.

Consequently, the work of constitution-making began without the participation of the League's elected representatives.

This situation revealed the failure of efforts to secure a common constitutional settlement acceptable to the principal competing organisations.

Attlee's announcement of 20 February 1947

On 20 February 1947, British Prime Minister Clement Attlee announced the intention to transfer power in British India no later than June 1948.

The announcement established a definite deadline for ending British rule.

Lord Mountbatten subsequently replaced Lord Wavell as Viceroy in March 1947 and was given responsibility for overseeing the final transfer of power.

Meanwhile, communal violence in Punjab and other regions increased the urgency of political negotiations.

The British government and major Indian political leaders moved towards accepting Partition as the means of completing the transfer of power.

Why the distinction between cause and consequence matters

Partition was not produced by a single riot, speech or political decision. It emerged from long-running disagreements over constitutional representation, the competing strategies of Congress and the League, the British role in transferring power and the violence of 1946–47.

Communal violence increased political pressure for a settlement. It also became one of the most tragic consequences of the division when the new borders were established.

Prelims focus

  • 16 August 1946: Direct Action Day called by the Muslim League.
  • Calcutta: Major communal riots during Direct Action Day.
  • 2 September 1946: Interim Government took office.
  • 9 December 1946: Constituent Assembly first met; the League boycotted.
  • 20 February 1947: Attlee announced transfer of power no later than June 1948.
  • Trap: The February 1947 announcement proposed a deadline; it did not itself establish India and Pakistan.

[NCERT, Our Pasts III, Class 8, Chapter 9, printed pp. 125–126; NCERT, Themes in Indian History Part III, Class 12, Understanding Partition, printed pp. 390–394; The Nehru Archive, Selected Works of Jawaharlal Nehru, Second Series, Volume 1, editorial note on the Interim Government, consulted 22 November 2026; UK Parliament, Hansard, Indian Constitution, 12 December 1946, and India: Transfer of Power, 3 June 1947, consulted 22 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: A two-track timeline shows political deadlock and communal violence converging on Attlee’s transfer-of-power deadline, followed by Mountbatten’s arrival.
pictures.caption: Political deadlock and communal violence accelerated the decision to transfer power.

title: Direct Action Day, Communal Violence and the Failure of Compromise

body:
Why the final Partition Plan was adopted

By 1947, repeated attempts to establish a common constitutional arrangement had failed. Congress and the Muslim League remained divided over the future structure of government, while communal violence and administrative uncertainty increased.

Lord Mountbatten, the last British Viceroy of India, conducted negotiations with Indian political leaders over the final transfer of power.

The resulting settlement is known as the 3 June Plan, also called the Mountbatten Plan.

The 3 June Plan of 1947

On 3 June 1947, the British government announced a plan permitting the transfer of power to 1 or 2 successor authorities according to the decisions taken under the proposed procedure.

In practice, the plan led to the division of British India and the creation of India and Pakistan.

The principal features included:

  • Acceptance of the possibility of Partition rather than insisting upon a single united constitutional settlement.
  • Procedures for deciding whether Punjab and Bengal should be divided.
  • Referendums or other prescribed decision-making procedures for certain territories.
  • Boundary commissions to determine the division of Punjab and Bengal.
  • An accelerated transfer of political power during 1947.

The 3 June Plan differed fundamentally from the Cabinet Mission Plan of May 1946. The earlier proposal attempted to preserve a united India; the later plan established procedures leading to separate successor states.

Partition of Punjab and Bengal

Punjab and Bengal were especially difficult to divide because both contained substantial populations belonging to different religious communities.

Under the 3 June Plan, the legislatures of these provinces were to meet in separate sections representing Muslim-majority and other districts.

If a majority of either section voted for provincial partition, the province would be divided.

Detailed boundaries would then be determined by boundary commissions, which were instructed to consider contiguous Muslim-majority and non-Muslim-majority areas along with other relevant factors.

The resulting provincial divisions created East Punjab and West Punjab, and West Bengal and East Bengal.

East Punjab and West Bengal became parts of India, while West Punjab and East Bengal became parts of Pakistan.

Other important territorial decisions

The final settlement also required decisions concerning other territories.

TerritoryDecision-making procedureResult
PunjabProvincial assembly sections and boundary commissionDivided into East Punjab and West Punjab
BengalProvincial assembly sections and boundary commissionDivided into West Bengal and East Bengal
North-West Frontier ProvinceReferendumJoined Pakistan
Sylhet district of AssamReferendum followed by boundary determinationMost of Sylhet joined East Bengal; part of the then Karimganj subdivision remained in India

These procedures show that Partition was not implemented through a single identical process in every region.

The Radcliffe Boundary Commissions

Sir Cyril Radcliffe chaired the boundary commissions responsible for determining the partition boundaries of Punjab and Bengal.

The commissions operated under severe time pressure. Their task was complicated by mixed populations, competing territorial claims and the economic and administrative connections between districts.

The Radcliffe Awards were announced on 17 August 1947, after the formal transfer of power.

Consequently, many people did not know the final position of the new international border when independence was celebrated.

Boundary announcement after independence

The formal transfer of power took place before the public announcement of the Radcliffe Awards. The legal creation of the new Dominions and the publication of their final provincial boundary decisions were therefore separate events.

The Indian Independence Act, 1947

The Indian Independence Act, 1947 received Royal Assent on 18 July 1947.

Section 1 provided for the establishment of 2 independent Dominions, India and Pakistan, from 15 August 1947, the statutory appointed day.

Pakistan commemorates its independence on 14 August, while India celebrates its independence on 15 August. This distinction should not be confused with the appointed day specified in the Act.

The Act also provided the legal framework for dividing Bengal and Punjab, establishing the new Dominions and transferring legislative authority.

Dominion status meant that the new states possessed independent governmental and legislative authority while initially retaining the British monarch as their constitutional head of state. India became a republic later, on 26 January 1950.

British Indian provinces and princely states

The division of British Indian provinces and the future of princely states were related but legally distinct matters.

British Indian provinces were territories directly administered under British authority. Their division was addressed through the Partition arrangements and the Indian Independence Act.

Princely states were ruled by Indian princes under British paramountcy. Section 7 of the Indian Independence Act provided that British paramountcy over these states would lapse on the appointed day.

This meant that the integration of princely states required separate political arrangements. Their territories were not automatically divided in the same manner as Punjab and Bengal.

Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, who hailed from Nadiad in Gujarat, played an important role in negotiations surrounding independence during 1945–47 and subsequently in the integration of princely states.

Prelims focus

  • 3 June 1947: Mountbatten Plan announced.
  • 18 July 1947: Indian Independence Act received Royal Assent.
  • 15 August 1947: Statutory appointed day for the establishment of 2 Dominions.
  • 17 August 1947: Radcliffe Awards announced.
  • Sir Cyril Radcliffe: Chairman of the Punjab and Bengal Boundary Commissions.
  • Trap: The lapse of British paramountcy over princely states was different from the partition of British Indian provinces.

[UK Parliament, Hansard, India: Transfer of Power, 3 June 1947, columns 35–40; Indian Independence Act, 1947, original enacted text, sections 1–7, legislation.gov.uk, consulted 22 November 2026; The National Archives, Partition of British India, sections on the announcement and boundaries, consulted 22 November 2026; NCERT, Politics in India since Independence, Class 12, Chapter 1, Challenges of Nation Building, printed pp. 8–14; NCERT, Our Pasts III, Class 8, Chapter 9, printed p. 124.]

pictures.alt: Timeline separates the Partition plan, Royal Assent, Pakistan’s commemoration, the statutory transfer of power and the later boundary awards.
pictures.caption: Political agreement, legislation, independence and border publication were distinct stages.

title: The 3 June Plan, Indian Independence Act and Partition Boundaries

body:
Partition as a political and human event

The Partition of British India in 1947 was more than the creation of 2 new countries. It caused widespread violence, migration, displacement and the separation of communities that had lived together for generations.

The division of Punjab and Bengal placed large religious minority populations on different sides of the new borders.

Although the Partition arrangements were based substantially on the principle of religious majorities, the population of British India could not be separated neatly into 2 religiously uniform territories.

Many Muslims continued living in India, while substantial Hindu and other minority populations remained in Pakistan.

Mass migration and displacement

As communal violence escalated, millions of people left their homes and travelled towards what they believed would be safer territory.

Many Hindus and Sikhs moved from areas incorporated into Pakistan towards India, while many Muslims moved from India towards Pakistan.

Migration was particularly intense in Punjab, where the movement of people across the newly established border took place amid severe violence and fear.

Population movements in Bengal followed somewhat different patterns and continued over a longer period in several areas.

Refugees often travelled on foot, by road and by railway. Many families arrived in unfamiliar places without adequate food, housing or financial resources.

Temporary refugee camps, relief arrangements and rehabilitation programmes became major responsibilities of the newly independent governments.

Deaths and the scale of displacement

The exact number of people who died or migrated during Partition cannot be stated with complete certainty. Historical estimates vary because of incomplete records and the disorder of the period.

One NCERT Class 12 account estimates that about 80 lakh people migrated across the new borders and that between 5 lakh and 10 lakh people were killed in Partition-related violence.

Other historical accounts provide different estimates. These numbers should therefore be treated as historical estimates rather than exact counts.

How to understand historical estimates

Population displacement and death figures depend on the geographical area, time period and evidence used in a particular estimate. A textbook estimate identifies the approximate scale of suffering; it does not establish an exact final number.

Communal violence and attacks on civilians

Partition-related violence included the killing of civilians, attacks on settlements and refugee convoys, destruction of property and the forced displacement of religious minorities.

Women were particularly vulnerable to abduction, sexual violence, forced conversion and forced marriage. Many children were separated from their families.

The violence did not affect only political leaders or armed organisations. Ordinary families bore much of the suffering.

Nevertheless, the period also witnessed examples of people protecting neighbours belonging to other religions, providing shelter and assisting families trying to escape violence.

These acts of assistance demonstrate that communal hatred did not determine every individual's behaviour.

Division of property and institutions

Partition created major administrative difficulties because the institutions of British India had to be reorganised between the new Dominions.

The division affected:

  • Government financial assets and liabilities.
  • Administrative personnel and government offices.
  • Military organisation and defence establishments.
  • Railway services, equipment and communications.
  • Public property and other government institutions.

Private property and individual livelihoods were also disrupted on a large scale. Refugees who had abandoned their homes often faced difficult questions concerning accommodation, compensation and rehabilitation.

Gandhi's efforts for communal peace

Mahatma Gandhi opposed communal violence and continued working for Hindu-Muslim harmony during the final months of British rule.

On 15 August 1947, Gandhi was in Calcutta, where he was working to restore communal peace rather than participating in the main independence celebrations.

He subsequently worked to reduce violence in Delhi and to defend the right of Muslims to remain in India as equal citizens.

In January 1948, Gandhi undertook his final fast in Delhi in an effort to restore communal harmony.

He was assassinated on 30 January 1948 by Nathuram Vinayak Godse.

Partition and the political identity of independent India

The Muslim League's two-nation argument treated Hindus and Muslims as distinct political nations. However, independent India did not adopt the position that citizenship should depend upon belonging to the Hindu religious majority.

Leaders such as Gandhi, Jawaharlal Nehru and Maulana Abul Kalam Azad supported the idea that India should belong equally to citizens of different religious communities.

The Indian Constitution subsequently established a political framework based on equal citizenship and constitutional protections rather than religious identity as a condition of membership in the nation.

This distinction is central to understanding the political consequences of Partition: the territorial division of British India did not require every person to migrate according to religion, nor did it make the population of either new state religiously uniform.

Understanding the full historical sequence

The history of communal politics and Partition shows a progression from demands for political safeguards to disagreements over the organisation of the future state.

The Muslim League was established in 1906; separate Muslim electorates were introduced in 1909; the Congress accepted separate electorates under the 1916 Lucknow Pact; the League adopted the 1940 Lahore Resolution; and the failure of the 1946 Cabinet Mission Plan was followed by communal violence and the adoption of Partition in 1947.

These developments were connected, but they were not identical. Separate electorates concerned the method of choosing representatives, provincial autonomy concerned the distribution of governmental powers, and Partition concerned the creation of separate sovereign political territories.

Prelims focus

  • 1947: Partition caused large-scale migration, communal violence and refugee rehabilitation problems.
  • Punjab and Bengal: Both provinces were divided.
  • 15 August 1947: Gandhi was in Calcutta working for communal harmony.
  • January 1948: Gandhi undertook his final fast in Delhi.
  • 30 January 1948: Gandhi was assassinated by Nathuram Godse.
  • Trap: Partition did not mean that all Muslims left India or that India became a state reserved for members of one religion.

[NCERT, Politics in India since Independence, Class 12, Chapter 1, Challenges of Nation Building, printed pp. 8–14; NCERT, Themes in Indian History Part III, Class 12, Understanding Partition, printed pp. 392–400; NCERT, Our Pasts III, Class 8, Chapter 9, printed pp. 124–126; The National Archives, Indian Independence Part Two, sections on creation of Pakistan and impacts of migration, consulted 22 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Partition displaced families and transformed everyday life across the new borders.
